Importance is a noun that describes how much something matters.

When something has importance, it means it carries weight — it has a real effect on people, events, or outcomes. Paying attention to it makes a difference. Ignoring it could lead to a problem, a loss, or a missed opportunity.

Think of it this way: if you could remove something from a situation and nothing would change, it has no importance. But if removing it would cause damage, confusion, failure, or loss — then it has importance.

For something to have importance, at least one of the following must be true:

  • It affects outcomes. A doctor washing their hands before surgery has great importance — skipping it can cause infection and death.
  • It carries value. Your passport has importance when you're travelling internationally — without it, you simply cannot proceed.
  • It influences decisions. The price of a house has importance when deciding whether to buy it.
  • It has an impact on people. A teacher's encouragement has enormous importance in shaping a student's confidence.
Importance Is a Matter of Degree

Importance is not just "yes or no" — it exists on a spectrum. Something can have:

  • Great / enormous / tremendous importance — it matters a lot; ignoring it could be catastrophic. (Drinking water has enormous importance for survival.)
  • Considerable importance — it matters significantly. (Sleep has considerable importance for your health.)
  • Some importance — it matters, but not critically. (Choosing the right pen has some importance for a calligrapher.)
  • Little / minor importance — it barely matters. (The colour of a stapler has little importance in an office.)
  • No importance — it doesn't matter at all. (The exact shade of blue on a private notebook has no importance to anyone else.)
Importance Is Often Relative — It Depends on Context

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: the same thing can have different levels of importance depending on who you are, what you're doing, or where you are.

Example: A sunny day has great importance to a farmer who needs to dry harvested crops, moderate importance to a child planning outdoor play, and almost no importance to an office worker who sits inside all day.

The thing itself (a sunny day) hasn't changed. But its importance changes with context.

This is why we often say "the importance of X for Y" or "the importance of X in a certain situation."
Importance Can Be Recognised or Overlooked

One key use of this word is to describe whether people see or acknowledge how much something matters — or whether they miss it.

  • Recognise / understand / appreciate / acknowledge the importance of something → You see clearly that it matters.

(She finally recognised the importance of regular exercise after her health scare.)

  • Underestimate / overlook / ignore / dismiss the importance of something → You fail to see how much it matters.

(He underestimated the importance of proofreading and submitted a document full of errors.)

  • Stress / emphasise / highlight the importance of something → You draw attention to the fact that it matters.

(The coach stressed the importance of teamwork before the final match.)

  • Attach importance to something → You personally decide to treat it as something that matters.

(She attaches great importance to punctuality in professional settings.)
How "Importance" Appears in Sentences — Patterns to Know

The word importance almost always appears in a few reliable patterns:

1. "The importance of [something]"
This is the most common structure. It introduces what matters.

  • The importance of honesty in a relationship cannot be overstated.
  • We discussed the importance of backing up your data.

2. "Of [great/little/no] importance"
This describes how much something matters.

  • This detail is of great importance to the investigation.
  • The colour of the file folder is of no importance.

3. "Give / attach / place importance to / on [something]"
This describes how much weight a person personally assigns to something.

  • Different cultures place different levels of importance on eye contact.
  • He gave little importance to what others thought of him.

4. "Stress / emphasise / underline the importance of [something]"
This is used when someone is making a point about what matters.

  • The doctor emphasised the importance of finishing the full course of antibiotics.
Words That Are Similar — and How They Differ

Understanding related words will sharpen your understanding of importance.

Significance
Very close to importance. "Significance" often refers to what something means or what it represents, whereas "importance" focuses more on what effect something has. In most everyday usage, they can be used interchangeably.

  • The significance of the date was not lost on anyone. (It carried deep meaning.)
  • The importance of the date was not lost on anyone. (Also correct; but here it leans slightly more toward "it mattered a great deal.")

Weight
"Weight" (when used figuratively) is close to importance, but it emphasises seriousness and gravity — how heavy or serious something feels.

  • His words carried great weight in the room. (They were taken seriously; they mattered.)

Value
"Value" focuses on worth — how much something is worth, whether in money, usefulness, or personal meaning. "Importance" focuses on impact. Something can have value without having great importance, and vice versa.

  • This old photograph has great value to me personally. (It is precious to me.)
  • This old photograph has great importance to historians. (It significantly affects our understanding of history.)

Relevance
"Relevance" means how closely connected something is to the topic or matter at hand. A relevant thing is one that applies; an important thing is one that matters. Something can be relevant but unimportant (loosely connected but not impactful), or important but seemingly irrelevant at first glance.

Consequence
"Consequence" focuses on results and effects — what happens because of something. "Importance" is broader. You can say something is important without specifying its consequences. But when something "is of great consequence," you're pointing specifically to its outcomes.

Importance can be claimed or disputed.
People and groups sometimes claim importance for things to draw attention to their cause or argument. Politicians stress "the importance of national security." Activists stress "the importance of environmental protection." Whether you agree or not, the word is being used to argue that something deserves more attention and resources.

"Self-importance" — a related noun
When the word is modified to self-importance, it means an exaggerated sense of how important oneself is — in other words, arrogance or pomposity. A self-important person acts as though they matter far more than they actually do. This is always a negative trait.

"Of importance" vs. "important"
The phrase "of importance" is simply a slightly more formal way of saying "important."

  • This is important. = This is of importance.
  • This is a matter of great importance. = This is a very important matter.

Importance is the quality of mattering — of having an effect, carrying value, or influencing outcomes in a meaningful way. It exists in degrees (from little to enormous), it is relative to context and perspective, and it can be recognised, dismissed, attached, stressed, or underestimated. The word is almost always used in phrases like "the importance of," "of great importance," or "attach importance to."

Whenever you use or read this word, ask yourself: important to whom? In what context? To what degree? Answering those three questions will always give you the full picture.
